blocks.h: Catching Attacks in Named Data Networking

blocks.p: One unsupervised Isolation Forest, trained only on clean traffic, that detects two different NDN attacks on emulated and simulated networks.

blocks.alt: Chart of attacker detection rate against attacker rate for Cache Pollution and Interest Flooding
blocks.caption: The paper's central result: the two attacks' detection floors are an order of magnitude apart.

blocks.p: Named Data Networking fetches content by name instead of talking to a host. Routers cache data and keep state for every pending request, which opens two attacks: Interest Flooding, which floods routers with requests for content that doesn't exist, and Cache Pollution, which fills caches with junk. No single threshold rule catches both. We wanted one detector that does, trained without ever seeing an attack.

One Isolation Forest, trained only on clean traffic, tested on two independent platforms across the same three topologies (tree, dumbbell and a DFN-style mesh): miniNDN, which emulates the network with the real NDN forwarding daemon, and ndnSIM, an ns-3 simulator. On ndnSIM we swept the attacker's rate across 297 runs to find the slowest attack each one can still be caught at. KS hypothesis tests and feature-ablation studies showed which features actually carry each attack.

blocks.alt: Three network topologies: tree, dumbbell and partial mesh
blocks.caption: The three topologies, used on both platforms.

blocks.p: The standard story says Interest Flooding blows up a router's Pending Interest Table. In our emulation it didn't: PIT size was statistically the same under attack: the forwarder rejects attack requests with NACKs, and the table drains between polls. The signal was in the NACK rate and the satisfaction ratio instead, which corrects the usual picture of this attack.

blocks.h2: The hard part: a model that learned failure was normal

blocks.p: Early on the detector caught almost nothing. The model wasn't the problem. 22.6% of our "normal" training samples were idle intervals that the logging code recorded as total failure, so the model learned that failure looks normal. With clean data the same model found the attacker 89-98% of the time.
A second fix made it robust to load. Absolute rate features flagged busy but healthy traffic as attacks, so we replaced them with ratios.

blocks.alt: Bar charts comparing false-positive rate and detection for absolute-rate and ratio features
blocks.caption: Ratio features cut false positives on a busier normal run from 41% to 2%, without losing detection.

blocks.p: At a realistic false-positive rate of about 2%, Cache Pollution stays detectable down to about 44 Interests per second per attacker, while Interest Flooding stays detectable down to about 1.8. The floors hold across all three topologies, including ones the model never trained on. Cache Pollution is volumetric, so it has to shout to be seen; Interest Flooding looks different, not just louder.

blocks.alt: Detection rate against attacker volume as a multiple of legitimate traffic
blocks.caption: Interest Flooding is caught at roughly normal volume; Cache Pollution needs about ten times it.

blocks.p: So the practical limit of anomaly detection here isn't peak accuracy at one attack rate. It's the floor: how quietly an attacker can operate before the detector loses them. The paper is under revision for a journal.

blocks.h: MIDAS: When a Road Sign Hijacks the Model

blocks.p: Reproducing an attack where one sign in the camera view flips a vision-language model's driving decision, then finding where the hijack lives inside the model.

blocks.alt: The same street scene before and after a red PROCEED sign is added
blocks.caption: Same scene, same question. Without the sign the model answers brake; with it, proceed.

blocks.p: MIDAS is our undergraduate major project, and it's ongoing. We're reproducing CHAI, a published attack where a readable sign in a driving scene (say, one that reads PROCEED) makes a vision-language model change its decision, on InternVL2.5 with CHAI's DriveLM scenes. So far the attack reproduces, but more weakly than the paper reports, and a linear probe on the model's hidden states can already tell when it is following the sign instead of the scene. We've also compared model sizes from 1B to 8B, and next we want to try activation steering as a defense.

blocks.h: SPYDER: One Photo, Hours of Footage

blocks.meta: research · Samsung Innovation Campus AI capstone · 2026

blocks.p: Find a person in low-resolution surveillance video from a single photo, and say "no match" honestly instead of always guessing.

blocks.alt: SPYDER command screen with camera tiles, a watchlist, an unverified alert and an activity feed
blocks.caption: The command screen from the UI prototype. Silhouettes stand in for faces: volunteer footage never leaves the collecting laptop.

blocks.p: On clean photos face recognition is close to solved: NIST reports error rates around 0.15% for the best systems. Surveillance footage isn't clean. Faces are small, blurred, compressed, dark and turned away, and the same models fall hard there (one drops from 65.2% to 29.9% rank-1 on real CCTV). A system that always returns its closest guess will hand an investigator the wrong person.
A complete pipeline: video in, faces detected (SCRFD), tracked, filtered by a quality gate, aligned and embedded, then matched.

list: Live Watch: armed subjects are matched in real time and raise one alert per appearance, with evidence.
Recorded Search: each video gets a cached FAISS index, and one photo returns ranked candidate tracks or "no match".
Three embedding models behind one interface (ArcFace R50, SFace, AdaFace IR-101), so they can be compared under identical conditions.
A calibrated threshold set from strangers' scores at a target false-alarm rate, so "no match" is a real answer.
31 REST endpoints plus a WebSocket event channel, 63 automated backend tests, and CI.

blocks.h2: Built to produce leads, not verdicts

blocks.p: Every candidate is marked unverified and needs a human to hold-to-confirm or reject. No raw live video is stored, only alert evidence (the best face and one frame), and expired data is garbage-collected. Volunteers gave written consent, and their data stays on the collecting machine.

blocks.alt: SPYDER sign-in screen with system status checks
blocks.caption: Sign-in: every action is written to an activity log under the operator's ID.

blocks.p: On a MacBook Air M2 with CoreML, face detection takes about 18 ms per frame and each embedding 3-5 ms. Indexing recorded video at 5 sampled frames per second runs about 7.5x faster than real time, so an hour of footage takes roughly 8 minutes, and searching a video's faces takes about 0.04 ms per query.
All software milestones are built and tested. What's left is the evaluation itself: recording the consented volunteer gallery and running the degradation, calibration and subgroup experiments.

with Aman Dhaubanjar and Ayush Kumar Jha

blocks.h: English to Nepali Translation, From Scratch

blocks.p: A 35M-parameter Transformer I wrote from the paper up and trained on a laptop, translating everyday English into fluent Nepali.

blocks.alt: The translator on Hugging Face Spaces translating an English sentence into Nepali
blocks.caption: My sentence, its real output. The demo sleeps when idle, so give it about a minute to wake.

blocks.p: I wanted to understand Transformers by building one with no translation library doing the hard parts: multi-head self and cross attention, sinusoidal positional encodings, the warmup learning-rate schedule, label smoothing. All of it is written by hand in PyTorch.

The first version translated Sanskrit to English, character by character. Ten epochs took about 18 hours on my M2 Air and produced phonetic mush. Around 80% of the attention compute was being spent on padding.

Switching to BPE tokens and length-bucketed batches made epochs about 12x faster and the English fluent, but the scores stayed in single digits. The model wasn't the problem. The corpus was 73k pairs of epic verse with loose, literary translations. In low-resource translation the data is the model, so I moved to a language pair with about 20 times more data and a standard benchmark.

list: An encoder-decoder Transformer: 4 + 4 layers, d_model 384, 8 heads, 35.0M parameters.
SentencePiece BPE with 16k pieces per language and byte fallback, so no word is ever unknown.
Data: NLLB's 19.6M mined English-Nepali pairs, cleaned and cut to the top 1M by LASER score.
Training: 6 epochs on an Apple M2 Air, about 2 hours each. Dev loss fell from 9.69 to about 4.55 with no overfitting.
Shipped as a Gradio app on Hugging Face Spaces.

blocks.p: On FLORES-200 devtest (1,012 unseen sentences, greedy decoding): BLEU 13.78, ChrF 41.22. ChrF is the fairer judge here, because Nepali's rich inflection makes BLEU's exact-word matching read low. Its best translations are near-human:

blocks.code:
EN  : In remote locations, without cell phone coverage, a satellite phone may be your only option.
REF : दुर्गम स्थानहरूमा, सेल फोनको कभरेज बिना, उपग्रह फोन तपाईंको एक मात्र विकल्प हुन सक्छ।
HYP : रिमोट स्थानहरूमा, सेल फोन कभरेज बिना, एक उपग्रह फोन तपाईंको मात्र विकल्प हुन सक्छ।
      BLEU 55.7 · ChrF 77.9

blocks.alt: Bar chart of sentence BLEU by source length bucket
blocks.caption: Sentence BLEU by source length: steady for everyday sentences, weaker on very short and very long ones.

blocks.p: It still drops rare compound terms and borrows English loanwords like रिमोट where a native word exists. Beam search and more epochs would close part of that gap.

blocks.h: Aakha: Walking Guidance for Blind Users

blocks.p: Turns a phone camera into short spoken cues for blind and low-vision walkers, with no LLM anywhere in the safety loop.

blocks.caption: Real street footage through the pipeline. Cyan is the walking corridor, yellow marks zebra stripes, and the top-left text is the cue it speaks.

blocks.p: A white cane finds what's at your feet. It doesn't tell you a scooter is closing in, or that a zebra crossing is right in front of you. And "is it safe to step forward" is the wrong question to hand to a large language model that can be slow or wrong. Aakha keeps the safety loop to classic computer vision and small, fast models.
The phone is the camera and the speaker. A laptop runs the pipeline, and the phone connects over a Cloudflare HTTPS tunnel by scanning a QR code.

list: YOLO11n with ByteTrack tracks objects every frame. Only things whose ground contact falls inside a walking corridor matter, so a bus across the road is ignored.
Collision cues come from how fast a tracked box grows: a looming object becomes "closing on person".
Depth Anything V2 runs in the background for walls, and classic CV finds zebra crossings (edges and Hough lines) and traffic-light colours.
One voice. Every part of the system posts to one priority queue, and exactly one consumer speaks, so cues never talk over each other. A soft beep means the path ahead is clear.
Hold to talk: offline Vosk speech recognition handles "read this" (on-device OCR), "what am I holding" and "repeat that".

blocks.h2: Designed to be used without sight

blocks.p: The whole phone screen is one button: tap to start or pause, hold to speak. There are no menus to find. Critical cues jump the queue but never cut off a sentence already playing, which can delay them a second or two, so every cue is kept short.

table: built most of the system (team of 3)
YOLO11n + ByteTrack (ONNX), Depth Anything V2, OpenCV, Vosk, FastAPI WebSockets, Android

blocks.h: Voice Bridge: Calls Without a Language Barrier

blocks.p: A video-calling app where each person speaks their own language and reads the other in theirs, as live captions.

blocks.alt: Voice Bridge sign-in screen: pick the language you speak and the language for captions
blocks.caption: You pick the language you speak and the one you want to read.

blocks.p: Two people who don't share a language should still be able to just call each other. In Voice Bridge the other person's words show up as captions in your language while they talk, and what you type in chat arrives in theirs.

list: Peer-to-peer WebRTC video and audio (plus screen share), signalled over Socket.io.
Each caller streams their own mic to a FastAPI backend over a WebSocket, as 16 kHz PCM from an AudioWorklet.
The backend finds speech with voice-activity detection, transcribes it locally with faster-whisper, translates it into the other caller's language and pushes it back as a caption.
Translation is free and offline by default with Argos Translate; Google Cloud Translation is an opt-in for higher quality.
Translated text chat rides the same WebSocket, with typing helpers like phonetic transliteration for Hindi, Arabic and Japanese.

blocks.alt: In-call view with a video tile, translated captions and a chat panel
blocks.caption: In-call view from a test call with fake camera devices: captions and translated chat on the right.

blocks.p: Two-party calls only, no auth, and state lives in memory, so a server restart drops the call. Captions arrive per phrase, after you pause, not word by word. Calls behind strict mobile NATs need TURN, so free relay servers are already wired in.

blocks.h: Kanun Sathi: Nepal's Law, With Sources

blocks.p: Ask a legal question in Nepali or English and get an answer grounded in the actual law, with the source cited.

blocks.alt: Kanun Sathi chat answering a Nepali question about dissolving parliament
blocks.caption: Asked in Nepali about dissolving parliament, it answers from the Constitution and lists the source.

blocks.p: Many young people in Nepal have no reliable way to check what the law actually says. They pick it up from social media or from elders answering from experience. Kanun Sathi answers in plain language from the Constitution, criminal law, family law and social regulations, and every answer names the document and article it came from, so people can check it themselves.

list: Built on Morphik, an open-source RAG framework, configured for Nepali.
Gemini 2.5 Flash writes the answers; we picked it because it handled Nepali better.
Embeddings run locally with Ollama's nomic-embed-text (768 dimensions), stored in PostgreSQL with pgvector.
Documents are chunked at 2,000 with 200 overlap; the original 6,000 kept overflowing the local model's context.
Prompts that enforce citations, so every answer points back to page-level sources in the law.
Ingestion runs in background workers (Redis + ARQ), so uploading a big document doesn't block the API.
A React + TypeScript frontend, and the whole stack (FastAPI, PostgreSQL/pgvector, Redis, Ollama) containerised with Docker Compose.

blocks.alt: Lawyer research view with document selection and a question box
blocks.caption: The research view: pick specific documents, then ask across just those.

blocks.h: Gym Guru: Five Minutes a Day, Better Form

blocks.p: A Flutter app that teaches one movement skill a day and coaches every rep through the camera.

blocks.alt: Four Gym Guru phone screens: form check, live set, results and skill path
blocks.caption: Form check, a live tracked set, results, and the skill path.

blocks.p: Most people quit training because sessions are long and nobody tells them their form is off. Gym Guru turns training into a short daily lesson: learn one skill like squat depth from a demo and three cues, practise a tracked set of 12 reps in front of the phone camera, then review a form score with errors flagged on the exact rep they happened.

It's a UI-complete prototype. Navigation, state and the whole lesson loop work. The camera feed and pose data are simulated: the skeleton is drawn from a depth curve, and scripted mistakes on rep 4 (knees cave in) and rep 9 (too shallow) exercise the coaching and results screens end to end.

blocks.alt: Five Gym Guru screens: goals, plan, today, progress and share
blocks.caption: Onboarding goals, the personal plan, today, progress and share cards.

list: Each flow owns one ChangeNotifier, so there are no state-library dependencies while the data model settles.
Fonts ship with the app and runtime font fetching is off, so it renders correctly with no network.
Next: real pose estimation on device (ML Kit or MediaPipe), local persistence, then accounts.

blocks.meta: Layman AI · intern, now Junior AI Engineer · 2026

blocks.p: Turning ordinary padel match footage into the things players and coaches actually ask about: who hit what, where everyone stood, and which points broke the rules.

blocks.alt: Animated padel rally with court zones, player IDs, rackets, pose and shot labels drawn over the footage
blocks.caption: One rally as the client sees it: every player tagged, every hit marked, every shot named.

blocks.p: Padel is filmed constantly, but almost nobody watches the footage twice. The client wanted that footage to become something useful without a person sitting through every rally with a notepad. Upload a match, get back the answers a coach or player would ask for: how many shots each person played, what kind, where they spent the match, how rallies started and ended, and when a point broke the rules. It had to run on their own machines, with their own models, and give results they could trust enough to show to paying players.
A backend the client runs themselves. They hand it a match video and get a folder back, named by date and match, with a short note explaining every file inside. For each match it produces:

list: An annotated match video. Every player keeps the same ID for the whole match, with rackets, body pose, court zones and walls drawn in, and each hit labelled with the shot type.
A clean tracking replay. The match redrawn on a plain court with stick-figure players and the ball's path, easy to read on a phone and free of the camera's clutter.
Shot by shot data. Who hit the ball, when and with which shot (serve, forehand, backhand, smash, bandeja or lob), ready to open in a spreadsheet or feed into an app.
Rallies and rule calls. Where each point started and finished, plus padel-specific faults such as a serve into the fence or a ball hitting the glass before the floor.
Charts. A heatmap of where each player stood, ball speed over the match and each player's mix of shots.
Players see their own match in numbers: how often they smash, how much they lean on the backhand, and whether they really stay at the net as much as they think.

Coaches jump straight to the moments worth talking about, such as every serve or every lost point, instead of scrubbing through an hour of video. Heatmaps make positioning problems obvious at a glance.
Clubs and the client's app get structured data for every match, so they can track a player over a season, compare players, or build highlight reels automatically.

blocks.p: The hardest part was making the numbers believable. In an early client demo the system counted hits that never happened. When I went through it frame by frame, more than a third of the hits it reported were the ball simply flying past a racket. I rebuilt the hit detection to look for the ball actually changing direction at a racket, then checked it against a minute of play I had labelled by hand. It now catches 78% of real hits, and on the far side of the court, where players look tiny, it finds 7 of 9 hits instead of 1.
